pr.title: Plan reviews that wait until a pull request is ready
pr.head: 8cd2d46f08a4bca3cd1b5255d01d8a5b60d71ec0

summary: Projector's review loop reviews pull requests on its own. A background process, the watch daemon, notices each commit pushed to a pull request and asks an agent session to review it. On your own pull request, GitHub won't let you approve or request changes, so Projector uses draft state as its verdict today. A review with findings turns the pull request into a draft, and a clean review marks it ready for review.

Because draft already means "not signed off", an author has no way to say "I'm still working on this". Every push gets a full review, including pushes the author replaces minutes later. This pull request adds a plan, docs/projects/review-on-ready, that gives draft back the meaning GitHub gives it. A pull request stays a draft while its author works, and gets its first review when the author marks it ready. Two labels, and in some repositories a commit status, then carry the verdict instead of draft state.
The pull request adds no code. The plan is marked ready, which claims that it answers or deliberately defers every question that would block building it.

cards.html:
TodayAfter
Which heads are reviewedEvery head of every covered pull requestUnder a repository subscription, only heads of pull requests that aren't drafts
Where the verdict showsDraft state on your own pull requestA clean label, and a reviewing label while a review runs
What blocks a mergeNothing Projector controlsA required projector/review commit status, only in a repository that opts in

Event to the fixing sessionDRAFT: a draft nobody here reviewsUNREVIEWED: a ready pull request nobody is reviewing

cards.title: Terms
cards.html:
• Repository subscription. A session asked to review every pull request of the operator's in a repository, through review-repo. Only these wait for ready.
  • Pull request subscription. A session asked to review one pull request, through review-pr. These review drafts too.
  • Signed off. The newest counted Projector verdict on the head is clean and no Projector finding thread is open (§ 2.2).
  • Start comment. The comment project review setup posts to say a review of a head is under way. The reviewing label follows it.
  • Hold. Today, a comment by the author that keeps a signed-off pull request in draft while the author builds a change. The plan replaces it with draft state alone.
  • Commit status and ruleset. A status is a pass or fail mark GitHub attaches to one commit. A ruleset can require one before a branch accepts a merge.

groups.title: The plan
groups.kicker: One new plan file that specifies the change, with nothing built yet
intro: The plan opens with the problem: one repository's pull request got 9 reviews over 26 commits, three of them clean verdicts in a row that layout changes replaced within minutes. § 2 is the design, and its subsections are where a reviewer's attention belongs. § 2.1 walks a pull request from opening to merge, § 2.2 defines when a head counts as signed off, § 2.3 lists exactly what Projector writes to GitHub, and § 2.6 lists how the daemon's events change.

§ 3 gives the reason for each decision, § 4 lists the acceptance criteria and the tests that must fail before the change, and § 6 covers rollout. § 7 lists four open questions, each deferred on purpose, which is what lets the plan claim ready.

checks.text: Read the plan against two kinds of subscription. A repository subscription skips draft heads, while a pull request subscription, the one review-pr creates, reviews drafts too. Both § 2.1's head rule and § 2.6's RESPONDED rule turn on that difference.

files.note: The whole change: a new plan, at status: ready and priority: now, for reviews that wait until a pull request is ready, with labels and an optional required status carrying the verdict.

checks.text: Steps 1 to 8 are the life of a pull request under the plan. Draft means the author is still working, ready means review it, and the labels and the status say what the newest review found. Step 6 is the hold's replacement: converting to a draft while the author builds a change on a signed-off head.

This is the rule publish uses for draft state today, without the hold. I read publish in review.py: it turns the pull request into a draft when the newest counted verdict requests changes, when a finding thread is open, or when a hold is open.

An existing label with the same name is used as it is. A repository whose own clean or reviewing label means something else turns the labels off with review.labels = false, and § 2.5 then has init skip the workflow too, so nothing removes that label.

The workflow can't run a fork's code with its write token. I read the job: it has no checkout step, and it passes the shell only the pull request number and the repository name. Its job-level if skips the job, so no runner starts, unless the clean label is present.

The status is required only where a ruleset says so. publish asks GitHub for the rules on the default branch and posts projector/review only when one requires it, so a workplace repository where people approve never sees a failing Projector check beside its CI.

The settings table here describes less than § 2.5 now does. The review.labels row doesn't say that false also makes init skip the workflow, and this row says true keeps the workflow in place, which holds only while the labels are on. The review suggests bringing the two rows in line.

This question is the only way a repository opts in to the required check. A yes creates a ruleset with no bypass actors, so even an admin can't merge a head that lacks a clean review. Projector's summaries go to refs/projector/summaries, not to a branch, so the ruleset doesn't block them.

With the labels off, nothing needs the workflow. init skips it wherever these steps would write it, because Projector adds no clean label then, and § 4 pins the case: init --require-review with labels off creates the ruleset and posts the status, and writes no workflow.

A draft that review-pr watches no longer stalls. The draft condition on RESPONDED now applies only under a repository subscription, so a pull request subscription asks for a re-review when the author declines a finding without pushing. I checked that the daemon can tell the two apart: route_review receives the subscription line, whose number is empty for a repository. § 4 covers the case with an acceptance row and a test_watch.py test.

The names this table replaces exist at this head. hold_add, hold_drop, hold_end, hold_lines, and HOLD_MARKER are in review.py, and route_review, route_fix, and is_held are in watch.py. The instructions block ships at version 24, so version 25 is the next one.

The verdict is computed twice today, as this bullet says. publish reads verdicts through verdicts, counted_reviews, and newest_verdicts in review.py, and the daemon has its own head_verdicts in watch.py. I found each one at this head.

Rollout needs the daemon and the skills to change together. Before upgrading, you end each open hold with today's hold --drop, and after upgrading you mark ready each open draft that was waiting on a review.

Ending a hold early is unsafe, and this step now says so. Today's daemon sends RESPONDED when a hold ends on an unchanged head, and an older publish then marks a clean pull request ready while its changes are still local. So a hold ends only once its push lands, as fix-pr requires, and a change that won't be built is dropped by its text. I read both behaviors in watch.py and review.py.
Each of the four open questions says it is deferred and why, which a plan at ready needs. I read each one against the design above, and none blocks building it.
